title: Pressure Profiling Technology
description: Deliberately varying brew pressure during extraction, from gentle pre-infusion ramps to declining profiles, to shape sweetness, body, and clarity in the cup.
facts: Pressure profiling means deliberately changing brew pressure at different stages of a shot instead of holding a flat 9 bars throughout.
A pre-infusion ramp wets the puck at 2-4 bar for several seconds before ramping to full pressure, reducing channeling and increasing sweetness.
A declining profile starts at 9 bar and drops to 6-4 bar as the shot progresses, reducing preferential water paths through the puck.
Manual lever machines like the Arco Viaggio give full physical control over pressure; the Arco Studio offers electronic pressure profiling with programmable, repeatable curves.

title: Water Chemistry Optimization
description: The mineral balance and total dissolved solids (TDS) of your water directly shape espresso extraction, flavor clarity, and machine longevity.
facts: Water makes up over 98% of every cup of espresso and is the single largest ingredient by volume.
The Specialty Coffee Association recommends a target TDS of 150 ppm, with an acceptable range of 75-250 ppm.
Hard water causes scale buildup that coats boilers and clogs solenoid valves, reducing heat-transfer efficiency over time.
Water that is too soft or pure becomes corrosive, slowly dissolving copper fittings and brass components.
A moderate mineral content with low alkalinity extracts well and protects equipment; activated carbon filters and remineralization packets both help achieve this balance.

title: Repairable, Serviceable Design

Arco machines are made from stainless steel, brass, and hardwood: materials that age with grace rather than planned obsolescence.
Arco designs for longevity, not replacement cycles, using durable materials and readily available service parts.
Sustainability starts with longevity: the greenest machine is the one that lasts a lifetime.

title: What is the difference between flat and conical burr grinders?
description: Flat burrs give a cleaner, more uniform grind and clarity in the cup; conical burrs run cooler and produce a fuller-bodied, more forgiving shot.
facts: Conical burrs use a cone-shaped inner burr inside a ring-shaped outer burr, operate at lower RPM, generate less heat and static, and produce a bimodal grind that creates a complex, forgiving, full-bodied cup, used in the Arco Preciso and Macinino.

Flat burrs use two parallel interlocking rings, run at higher RPM, and produce a more uniform unimodal grind that yields cleaner, more transparent flavor clarity, used in the Arco Zero and Macinino Pro.
Choose conical burrs for body, sweetness, and a forgiving brewing window; choose flat burrs for clarity, brightness, and tasting terroir.

title: How often should I clean and descale my espresso machine?
description: Clean daily with a wipe and flush, backflush weekly with a chemical cleaner, and descale every two to three months depending on water hardness.
facts: Daily: wipe the gasket and shower screen, flush a blank shot of water, and wipe the steam wand immediately after use.
Weekly: perform a chemical backflush with a dedicated cleaner like the Arco Cleaning Kit's backflush detergent, then rinse with several plain-water flushes.
Every two to three months: descale to remove mineral buildup from boilers and internal tubing; frequency depends on water hardness.
Coffee oils oxidize and turn rancid within hours of contact with metal, so regular cleaning is the single most important thing you can do to protect flavor and machine longevity.

title: Why does water quality matter for espresso?
description: Water makes up over 98% of espresso, and its mineral balance directly affects extraction, flavor clarity, and how long your machine lasts.
facts: The Specialty Coffee Association recommends a TDS target of 150 ppm, with an acceptable range of 75-250 ppm, for espresso.
Magnesium binds more readily to fruity, bright acids, while calcium enhances body and sweetness; the balance between them shapes flavor.
Hard water causes scale buildup in boilers and valves; water that's too soft or pure is corrosive to copper and brass components.
A purpose-built filtration system (activated carbon plus ion-exchange resin) or a remineralization recipe is the simplest path to well-balanced water.

title: How do I dial in a new bag of espresso beans?
description: Start with a fixed 18g dose at a 1:2 ratio in 25-30 seconds, then adjust grind size based on taste.
facts: Start with 18 grams of coffee in a standard double basket, distributed evenly and tamped with consistent pressure.
Target a 1:2 ratio (18g in, 36g out) in approximately 25 to 30 seconds; if it runs faster, grind finer, if it chokes, grind coarser.
Sourness and thin body signal underextraction (grind finer or increase yield); bitterness and a hollow finish signal overextraction (grind coarser or pull shorter).
Change only one variable at a time and keep a log of dose, grind setting, yield, time, and tasting notes to speed up the process.

title: Should I use single-origin coffee or a blend for espresso?
description: Blends are more forgiving and consistent for daily use; single origins reward careful dialing-in with a distinctive, transparent flavor.
facts: Single-origin espresso showcases the unique character of one farm or region but can be unforgiving: small shifts in dose or time push the shot off balance, and availability changes seasonally.
Blends combine multiple origins so their strengths complement each other, producing a more forgiving, consistent shot across seasons.
A good approach: use a reliable blend as your daily driver and treat single origins as weekend exploration when you have time to dial in.
Pair lighter single origins with flat-burr grinders like the Arco Zero for clarity, and lean on conical burrs like the Arco Preciso for body with blends.

title: How does pressure profiling improve espresso extraction?
description: Varying brew pressure during a shot, instead of holding a flat 9 bars, can increase sweetness, reduce bitterness, and smooth out mouthfeel.
facts: A pre-infusion ramp wets the puck at 2-4 bar for several seconds before ramping to full pressure, reducing channeling risk and promoting even extraction.
A declining profile starts at 9 bar and drops to 6-4 bar as the shot progresses, often increasing sweetness and reducing bitterness.
Manual lever machines like the Arco Viaggio give full physical control over pressure; the Arco Studio offers electronic pressure profiling with saveable, repeatable curves.

title: Can I bring my espresso setup when traveling?
description: Yes: a manual lever portable like the Arco Viaggio plus a hand grinder makes a self-contained, sub-1kg travel espresso kit that needs no electricity.
facts: Manual lever portables like the Arco Viaggio generate pressure through a hand-operated piston, need no electricity, and fit in a carry-on bag.
A hand grinder like the Arco Viaggio Grinder pairs with a portable machine for a fully self-contained setup weighing under a kilogram.
Grinding beans into single-dose vacuum-sealed containers before departure buys three to five days of reasonable freshness.
Bottled water around 100-150 ppm TDS is a safe travel choice; avoid distilled or heavily softened water, which underextracts.

title: How do I steam milk for latte art at home?
description: Stretch cold milk below 40°C to incorporate air, then texture between 55-65°C to build stable, glossy microfoam.
facts: Stretching (introducing air) should happen while milk is still below 40°C, when whey proteins are flexible enough to stabilize new bubbles.
Texturing (creating a vortex to break bubbles down to microfoam) works best between 55-65°C, where lactose sweetness and foam stability peak.
Past 70°C, whey proteins aggregate irreversibly, the foam turns coarse and stiff, and a sulfurous off-flavor develops with no way to recover it.
Whole milk foams most forgivingly for beginners and latte art; oat milk is the plant-based alternative that steams most similarly to dairy.

title: What is the difference between washed, natural, and honey processed coffee?
description: Washed coffee is clean and bright, natural coffee is sweet and fruit-forward, and honey processing lands in between.
facts: Washed processing removes the cherry skin and fruit within hours of picking, producing clarity, brightness, and defined acidity for precise, transparent espresso shots.
Natural processing dries the whole cherry intact for two to four weeks, letting fruit sugars migrate into the bean for intense sweetness, heavy body, and bold fruit flavors.
Honey processing leaves some mucilage on the bean during drying (classified white, yellow, red, or black honey by the amount retained), balancing washed clarity with natural sweetness.
Naturals are forgiving of a slightly coarse grind and work well as the base of espresso blends; washed coffees reward careful, precise extraction.
